newsitem.title: JAPAN: SOCCER-JAPAN PASSES CONTROVERSIAL LOTTERY BILL.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-JAPAN PASSES CONTROVERSIAL LOTTERY BILL.

text.p: Japan's parliament passed legislation on Tuesday to kick off a controversial J.League soccer lottery designed to raise money for sports promotion.

Having been approved by parliament's Lower House, the legislation should pass the Upper House in June. This would allow the lottery to begin in 1999 and end a battle between proponents and opponents that has already dragged on for seven years.

The bill, submitted by a bipartisan group of legislators and backed by the Japan Olympic Committee, could raise up to 200 billion yen ($1.72 billion) a year through sales of tickets with stakes on J.League match results.
Tickets would be sold at financial institutions for 100 yen ($0.86) with winnings pegged to the percentage of correct guesses on outcomes of twice-weekly J.League matches.
Half the net profits from the lottery would be used to promote sports, including training programmes and stadium construction, while the rest would go into state coffers.
The scheme has been modelled on the football pools in Italy, which have become a national institution and raised millions of dollars for professional sport.

While proponents say the lottery funds could help reverse Japan's long decline in Olympic medal counts and other international competitions, the plan is under fire from lawyers and women's groups, who say it will do more to stimulate gambling than sport.
The 100-yen tickets, cheaper than the price of a can of soft drink, would draw young people to gambling, which is banned in Japan, the Japan Federation of Bar Associations said in a statement.
The Ministry of Education, which would oversee the soccer lottery through subordinate public-sector firms, would in effect become a bookmaker, the opponents say.

Decades of massive pork-barrel spending, the product of political parties' heavy reliance on the construction industry, have already studded even remote areas of the Japanese countryside with sports arenas and other expensive public facilities of dubious utility, critics add.

But lottery proponents argue that government funds for sports are inadequate and will shrink further as Japan's recent economic slowdown has taken a heavy toll on tax revenues and the government is under pressure to cut spending. ($1=116 yen)
